bloques.titulo: What you will learn this week

bloques.html:
• Take an argument apart: claim, reasons, evidence, counterclaim, rebuttal.
  • Evaluate an argument: which parts are well supported, and which are weak.
  • Recognize persuasive techniques and say what each one does to the reader.
  • Write in formal register, and use modal verbs to make claims as strong as your evidence allows.
  • Write an opinion text with a counterclaim and a rebuttal.
  • Debate: defend a position aloud and answer an objection.

1. The five parts of an argument

Part What it is Typical words
Claim the position the writer wants you to accept I believe that, ... should, ... must not
Reason why the claim is right The first reason is, because, in addition
Evidence a fact, number, example or expert that supports a reason for example, according to, studies show
Counterclaim what the other side says Some people argue that, supporters claim, admittedly
Rebuttal the writer's answer to the counterclaim However, nevertheless, even so, that may be true, but

A writer who includes the counterclaim is not being weak. It shows that the writer has listened to the other side and can still answer it.

2. Evaluating an argument

Do not ask only "Do I agree?" Ask:

  • Is each reason supported by evidence? A reason with no evidence is only an opinion.
  • Is the evidence relevant? It has to be about this reason, not about something else.
  • Is it enough? One cousin or one neighbor is a single case, not proof.
  • Is there a weak move? Watch for: everybody knows... (no evidence), attacking people and not ideas, exaggeration (always, never, totally), and a counterclaim that is mentioned but never answered.

3. Persuasive techniques

Technique Example What it does to the reader
Rhetorical question Should we really wait any longer? Makes you answer in your head the way the writer wants
Emotive language a lonely experiment Makes you feel before you think
Rule of three air, water and food Sounds complete and is easy to remember
Direct address Imagine you are... Pulls you into the situation
Contrast pair we lose a machine / we lose lives Makes the difference between two things sharp
Statistic or expert seven months each way Makes the claim sound checked and reliable

A technique is not evidence. A good reader enjoys the technique and still asks for the evidence.

Language box — Formal register and modal verbs

Formal register is the language of essays, reports and debates.

Informal Formal
kids, guys children, students, people
don't, can't, it's do not, cannot, it is
tons of, a lot of many, a large amount of, a great deal of
'cause, so because, therefore, consequently
totally pointless, a waste of time unnecessary, not a productive use of time
I reckon, I guess I believe, in my view, it can be argued that

Modal verbs show how sure you are. Choose the one your evidence can support.

Strength Modal verbs Example
certain will, must, cannot A crew will need air and water.
advice or duty should, ought to Robots should go first.
possible may, might, could The tools could help other species.

A careful writer prefers could help some to will save all. A cautious claim is harder to attack.

Linking words for arguments: first, in addition, for example, consequently, therefore (to build your side) · admittedly, some people argue that (to bring in the other side) · however, nevertheless, even so (to answer it) · in conclusion, for these reasons (to finish).

4. Plan for an opinion text

  1. Introduction: the question and your claim in one clear sentence.
  2. Reason 1 + evidence (fact or example).
  3. Reason 2 + evidence.
  4. Counterclaim + rebuttal: Some people argue that... However,...
  5. Conclusion: say your claim again in new words. No new reasons here.

Vocabulary of the week

Word Meaning Word Meaning
claim the position a writer defends counterclaim the argument of the other side
rebuttal an answer that shows why a counterclaim is weaker to concede to admit that the other side is right about something
relevant connected to the point being made to support to give reasons or evidence for an idea
register the level of formality of language motion the statement that a debate is about
admittedly used when you accept a point from the other side nevertheless in spite of that
to divert to send something in a different direction threatened in danger of disappearing
extinct no longer existing anywhere crew the people who work on a ship or spacecraft

Read the text. The examples refer to it.

Send the Robots First (opinion article; text created for this guide)

Should the next footprints on Mars belong to a person? Not yet. I believe that robots should explore Mars thoroughly before any human crew is sent.

The first reason is safety. A journey to Mars takes about seven months each way, and the crew would need air, water and food for the whole trip, with no chance of rescue. If a robot breaks down, we lose a machine. If a spacecraft with people breaks down, we lose lives.

The second reason is that robots are already doing the job. Rovers such as Curiosity and Perseverance have driven across Mars for years, drilling into rocks and sending data home.

Admittedly, supporters of human missions argue that a trained person can explore far faster than any machine. That is true. However, speed matters little if the crew cannot survive. Robots can find water and test equipment first, so that people arrive later and more safely.

Exploration is not a race. Let the machines go first, and let the people follow when the road is ready.

Example 1 (claim). What is the writer's claim? → It is the sentence with "I believe that": robots should explore Mars thoroughly before any human crew is sent. Notice that the writer does not say people should never go.

Example 2 (reasons and evidence). → Reason 1: safety. Evidence: the trip takes about seven months each way, and a crew needs air, water and food for the whole trip, with no chance of rescue. Reason 2: robots already do the job. Evidence: the rovers Curiosity and Perseverance, named with what they do.

Example 3 (counterclaim and rebuttal). → Counterclaim: "supporters of human missions argue that a trained person can explore far faster than any machine." The writer concedes ("That is true") and then rebuts: "However, speed matters little if the crew cannot survive."

Example 4 (technique and effect). "If a robot breaks down, we lose a machine. If a spacecraft with people breaks down, we lose lives." → A contrast pair, with two sentences built the same way. Effect: the reader compares "a machine" with "lives" and feels the difference at once.

Example 5 (evaluate). Which part of the argument is weakest? → The last paragraph. "Exploration is not a race" sounds good, but it is a slogan, not evidence. Also, the writer never says how long "thoroughly" would take, so a critical reader may ask: How will we know when the robots have done enough?

Example 6 (formal register). Rewrite: "Sending people to Mars right now is a totally crazy idea 'cause it's way too risky." → Sending people to Mars at present would be unwise because the risks are too great.

Example 7 (modal verbs). Which is the most cautious claim? (a) Robots will find water on Mars. (b) Robots might find water on Mars. (c) Robots must find water on Mars. → (b): might says it is possible, not certain.

Example 8 (a short opinion text). Should homework be banned? → Homework should not be banned, but it should be shorter. (claim) First, a short task helps students remember what they learned that day; for example, ten minutes of practice keeps a new method fresh. (reason + example) In addition, working alone teaches students to organize their time. (reason) Admittedly, some people argue that children need their evenings to rest. However, a short task leaves plenty of time for rest and play. (counterclaim + rebuttal) For these reasons, schools should reduce homework and not remove it. (conclusion)

Read the letter and answer questions 1 to 8.

Ban Homework Now! (letter by a student; text created for this guide)

Homework is totally pointless and everybody hates it. My cousin stopped doing homework and he is fine. After seven hours of school, children need time to play, read and sleep; a tired student learns less the next day. Teachers who give homework obviously don't care about kids. Some people say homework teaches responsibility. Whatever. Ban it now!
Write the writer's claim in one sentence, in formal register.
One reason in the letter is supported by logic that a reader could accept. Copy it.
"My cousin stopped doing homework and he is fine." Why is this weak evidence?
"everybody hates it": what is wrong with this as support for the claim?
Which sentence attacks people and not their ideas?
The letter mentions a counterclaim. Copy it. Does the writer rebut it?
Replace "Whatever." with a real rebuttal of one or two sentences.
Which is the stronger argument, this letter or Example 8? Give two reasons.
Go back to "Send the Robots First".
Find a rhetorical question and a rule of three. Explain the effect of one of them.
Write one question that a critical reader could ask about the second reason.
Language.
Rewrite in formal register: (a) Zoos are kind of sad and kids don't learn tons there. (b) I reckon we can't just ignore this stuff.
Order these from the most cautious to the most certain: Chess will make you smarter. / Chess might make you smarter. / Chess should make you smarter.

Complete with however, therefore, admittedly or for example: (a) , robots are slower than people. , they do not need air or food. (b) The trip is long and dangerous. , robots should go first. (c) Rovers have made real discoveries. , they have drilled into rocks and studied them.
Writing and speaking.
Should every student learn to play chess at school? Write an opinion text of 8 to 10 sentences using the five-part plan.
Ask an adult to disagree with your text from question 14. Listen to the objection, repeat it in your own words ("You are saying that..."), and then answer it.

Challenge mission — Argue the other side. Choose something you believe strongly (for example, "dogs are better than cats" or "weekends should have three days"). Now write the strongest argument you can for the opposite side: a claim, two reasons and one piece of evidence. You are not allowed to make it weak on purpose. Then write the rebuttal you would give. Debaters call this "steelmanning": if you can state the other side's best case, your own answer becomes much harder to beat.
1. For example: Homework should be abolished. / Schools should stop giving homework.
1. "After seven hours of school, children need time to play, read and sleep; a tired student learns less the next day."
1. It is a single case. One person does not show what happens to students in general, and "he is fine" is vague.
1. It is an exaggeration with no evidence, and even if it were true, disliking something does not prove that it is useless.
1. "Teachers who give homework obviously don't care about kids."
1. "Some people say homework teaches responsibility." No. "Whatever" is not an answer.
1. For example: However, responsibility can also be learned through chores, sports or music practice, which do not make the school day longer.

1. Example 8 is stronger: every reason has an example or an explanation; it answers the counterclaim; it uses formal language and does not attack anyone; its claim is more cautious (shorter homework, not a ban).

1. Rhetorical question: "Should the next footprints on Mars belong to a person?" It makes the reader curious and prepares the answer "Not yet." Rule of three: "air, water and food". Three items sound complete and are easy to remember, so the needs of the crew stay in the reader's mind.
1. For example: If robots are already doing the job, what can they not do that a person could? or How much have the rovers discovered compared with what a human crew might find?
1. (a) Zoos can be distressing places, and children do not learn a great deal there. (b) In my view, this problem cannot simply be ignored.
1. Chess might make you smarter. → Chess should make you smarter. → Chess will make you smarter.
1. (a) Admittedly / However (b) Therefore (c) For example.
1. Check with the plan: claim, two reasons with evidence, counterclaim and rebuttal, conclusion; formal register; linking words.
1. The adult checks that you repeated the objection correctly before you answered it.
Challenge mission: show both texts to an adult. The mission is complete only if the adult cannot tell which side you really believe.
